actors: Norway's sovereign wealth fund (Government Pension Fund Global)
key_facts: Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement, funded with £2bn diverted from the existing National Wealth Fund.

Treasury internal modelling estimates that, had North Sea receipts of £200bn been invested without withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's, the fund would be worth about a trillion pounds.
Norway's fund holds about $2.4tn, draws down around 3% of its value annually, and must invest abroad; the UK fund is designed to invest domestically in green energy.
UK national debt reached £3tn for the first time in the same week; UK energy tax revenues are forecast to decline as North Sea production slows.
importance_reason: Новость о создании фонда на £2bn и ретроспективная модель с «триллионом» — важна для контекста политики, но без прямого немедленного рыночного эффекта; «триллион» — внутренняя оценка-гипотеза, а не факт.

actors: Cassie and Jon (Airbnb hosts, Georgia, US)
key_facts: Airbnb has updated its rules to limit what hosts may ask guests to do, including cleaning tasks. Hosts can set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb states that guests, who are required to pay a cleaning fee, should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds. The new rules apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November.

Hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes". Exceptions may be granted, e.g., limiting shower time under local drought-related water restrictions.

Contracts are allowed only in limited circumstances (e.g., when required by law or homeowners association rules). Hosts cannot impose fines; requests not following Airbnb policy are flagged and owners can appeal.
importance_reason: Platform policy change affecting hosts and guests; no direct market-wide or macro effect.

key_facts: More than one in 10 UK university students now plan to move abroad after graduating, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey of 15,000 final-year students.

According to the ISE, UK employers receive on average 140 applications per graduate vacancy, a 14% increase from 2025 and up from 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago; competition for graduate jobs is at a three-decade high.

Australia remains the most popular destination for British adults moving abroad overall; the Working Holiday Maker programme allows British passport holders aged 18-35 to live there for up to three years.
ONS figures show around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged 16-34, and 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived.

The US is the second most popular destination for British adults; a PhD candidate at Yale reports a salary of $51,000 a year (about to rise to $52,000), compared with funded UK PhD stipends of about £21,000.
importance_reason: Feature-style lifestyle and migration piece with some labour-market statistics; no market-moving event.
